payload.system: Return only the requested structured result. Act as a skeptical but fair reader and compare the book with the strongest specific alternative explanation.

messages.content:
You are the skeptical-reader judge in the final stage of a blinded experiment.
Independent agents have already found that the book's conclusion diverges from
a recognizable common interpretation. Your task is comparative: after reading
the book's sources and full argument, determine which specific interpretation
best explains the supplied scriptural evidence.

TERM

BOOK ENTRY
A prophecy given in advance — often a prophet's lived story — whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 7:14; Ezek 24:24; Luke 11:30) · see Signs and Similitudes, ch. 3

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 7:14 — Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Ezekiel 24:24 — Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign: according to all that he hath done shall ye do: and when this cometh, ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD.
Luke 11:30 — For as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation.

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

How did Paul read the Old Testament?
Not by a revelation the rest of us lack — he tells us his method outright, in the middle of a passage about Israel’s wilderness history:

Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.

The King James’ “ensamples” is the Greek typos — types, patterns struck in advance — and mark the two verbs: the things “happened” as types before they were “written” as types (so too 1 Corinthians 10:6).
Paul is not decorating history with lessons; he is telling us what the history is: composed.
And watch him work the method on text after text: the rock that followed Israel — “that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4); Adam — “the figure of him that was to come” (Romans 5:14); Abraham’s two households — “which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants” (Galatians 4:22-24), real women, real sons, and at the same time a composed likeness.
Paul is the proof that this is a method of reading and not a private gift: he points at scrolls everyone owned and demonstrates what was always in them.

So far this book has let Scripture define its symbols one word at a time — the seed is the word, the ground is the heart — but Paul read whole lives that way, because God writes with more than words: with wonders, with scenes, and with the lives of real men.
Scripture claims nothing less for the whole canvas.

All of creation testifies: “The heavens declare the glory of God… There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard” (Psalm 19:1-3; so Romans 1:20).
And all of history testifies: the psalm that recounts Israel’s whole story opens, “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old” (Psalm 78:2) — the very line Matthew lays over the parables of Jesus (Matthew 13:35), the psalm the last chapter took its exam under.
A history that can be called a parable is a history that was composed.

Scripture has two words of its own for that larger writing — sign and similitude — and this chapter defines them the same way the last chapter derived the seed and the ground: by letting Scripture use them in front of us.

Men who demand signs mean one thing by the word; the prophets mean another.
The demand is for a wonder performed on the spot.
But watch what Scripture calls a sign, and notice that there is no wonder in it anywhere.

When Samuel anointed Saul, he sent him home with signs: two men would meet him by Rachel’s tomb and tell him the lost donkeys were found; three men would meet him at the plain of Tabor carrying three kids, three loaves, and a bottle of wine, and would hand him two loaves; then a company of prophets would come down from the high place (1 Samuel 10:2-6).
Travelers on a road, a greeting, bread changing hands — scenes told in advance, down to the count of the loaves.

And it was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and all those signs came to pass that day.

Nothing was conjured; everything foretold simply happened.
A sign is a word given ahead of events, and its proof is that it comes true.
And a sign can be more than a spoken word — it can be a prophet:

Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign: according to all that he hath done shall ye do: and when this cometh, ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD.

Not Ezekiel’s sermon — Ezekiel, the man; his acted story; “all that he hath done.”
Isaiah and his message-named children were “for signs and for wonders in Israel” (Isaiah 8:18), and Isaiah himself walked out one prophecy barefoot for three years “for a sign” (Isaiah 20:3).

The pattern holds into the gospels: the shepherds are given “a sign” that is simply a scene to find — “Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger” (Luke 2:12) — and Simeon calls the child himself “a sign which shall be spoken against” (Luke 2:34).
It holds to the last book of the Bible, whose visions are titled signs: the travailing woman is “a great wonder” — the Greek is sēmeion, a great sign — “in heaven” (Revelation 12:1), and so is the dragon that waits on her (Revelation 12:3).

Gather the uses and the definition writes itself: a sign is a message given ahead of time — an oracle, a scene, or a prophet’s own lived story — so that its fulfillment testifies.
A wonder on demand is what men ask for; a sign is what God gives.

Now test the definition on the most famous sign in the Bible:

Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

Is this sign not a miracle?
Its fulfillment is.
But mark what happened on the day the sign was given: nothing.
No wonder was performed in Ahaz’s court; the word itself was the sign, and it stood as the sign for seven centuries before its fulfillment arrived to testify.
The miracle belongs to the fulfillment; the sign is the message that ran ahead of it.

There is a second family of signs, and it does not point forward at all: it points to a standing covenant.
The bow in the cloud is “the token of the covenant” (Genesis 9:12-13 — a chapter of its own ahead); circumcision is “the sign… a seal of the righteousness of the faith” (Genesis 17:11; Romans 4:11); the Passover blood on the houses was “a token” (Exodus 12:13); the word of God itself is bound “for a sign upon thine hand” (Deuteronomy 6:8); and the sabbath is “a sign between me and you throughout your generations… that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you… a sign… for ever” (Exodus 31:13, 17; Ezekiel 20:12).
A sign, then, is God’s mark set on a message or on a covenant — and the covenant-signs are declared perpetual.

Moses himself gives the tests of a valid sign, and there are two.
The first is fulfillment: “if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:21-22) — a sign that fails is no sign, and the prophet who gave it spoke presumptuously.
But fulfillment alone is not enough, and the second test overrides the first: if a prophet gives a sign “and the sign or the wonder come to pass,” yet he teaches you to go after other gods, you shall not hearken — “for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).
To go after other gods is no separate offense standing beside lawbreaking; it is the first commandment broken — the head of the law — and Deuteronomy draws that conclusion itself in the next verse: “keep his commandments, and obey his voice” (Deut 13:4).
A valid sign must both come true and come from one who does not teach against the law.
A fulfilled sign never licenses lawbreaking; God Himself may send one as the proving.

The second word comes from God’s own mouth:

I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets.

A similitude is a likeness — but not a likeness drawn in words, like a parable.
God says He used similitudes by the ministry of the prophets: He composed likenesses out of lives.
The prophet who wrote that line was himself the proof — his whole life a sign.

Hosea’s book opens with the command:

Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD.

The interpretation is handed down in the same breath as the command.
His children were message-named like Isaiah’s: Lo-ruhamah, Not-pitied; Lo-ammi, Not-my-people (Hosea 1:6, 9).
And when the wife was lost to her adulteries, the command came again: “Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel” (Hosea 3:1) — and the prophet bought his own bride back for fifteen pieces of silver (Hosea 3:2).
A marriage, a betrayal, a redemption — lived out over years, so that Israel could watch the love of the LORD walk through town.
This is the writing Paul learned to read — the typos that “happened unto them” — and it runs beyond lives into the covenant's own patterns: the law is “a shadow of good things to come” (Hebrews 10:1), the tabernacle built “according to the pattern” of heavenly things (Hebrews 8:5).

Jesus reads history the same way, time after time: “as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be” (Matthew 24:37); “as it was in the days of Lot… even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed” (Luke 17:28, 30); “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” (John 3:14).
He does not treat the histories as illustrations that happen to fit.
He treats them as prophecies that must be fulfilled.

The New Testament ratifies the method instance after instance, in so many words.
The manna was a similitude of “the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32) — and the feeding of the five thousand that opens that discourse is itself a lived sign: John calls it one (the “miracle” of John 6:14 is the Greek sēmeion), the sign the last chapter read in full — the Law carried by witnesses, feeding the famished — and the Sea & Waters chapter ahead will deepen the fish’s half of its key.

The temple was a similitude of “the temple of his body” (John 2:19-21); the Passover lamb, of “Christ our passover… sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7) — John even cites the lamb-rule “a bone of him shall not be broken” (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46) as fulfilled prophecy.
A past man prophesied a future man: “this is Elias, which was for to come” (Matthew 11:14).
And Peter calls baptism the “like figure” of the flood (1 Peter 3:21) — his Greek word is antitypon: type and antitype are Scripture’s own vocabulary, not a scholar’s invention.

How far may this be carried?
But the risen Lord’s own claim outruns any cautious answer:

And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.

He said as much elsewhere: “Moses… wrote of me” (John 5:46).
Not a proof-text here and there: all the scriptures.

How can real history be prophecy?
Solomon gives the warrant, and it is the epigraph over this chapter: “The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be… and there is no new thing under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 1:9).

Read flat, it sounds like world-weariness.
But the sun is a symbol with a chapter of its own ahead — “the LORD God is a sun” (Psalm 84:11) — and under that Sun, the saying turns from a sigh into a signature: under the Father’s hand there is no new thing, because history is composed, and the Composer repeats His themes on purpose.
Solomon says it again with the veil pulled back:

That which hath been is now; and that which is to be hath already been; and God requireth that which is past.

God requires the past — summons it back, calls for the pattern again.
What has been done will be done again, because the same Author is writing.
That is why a life can be a prophecy: the first telling is the similitude, and God will require it.

God says to Abraham:

Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.

Mark three things in that one verse.
It is the first time the word love appears in all of Scripture — and the Bible’s first love is a father’s love for the son he must offer.
The son is “thine only son” — the very phrase Hebrews keeps: Abraham “offered up his only begotten son” (Hebrews 11:17).
And the place is chosen by God: the land of Moriah — the mountain where the temple would stand, “the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3:1).

Now the scenes run.
“On the third day” Abraham lifts up his eyes and sees the place (Genesis 22:4).
The wood of the offering is laid on the son, and the son carries it up the hill (Genesis 22:6) — as another Son, on that same ridge, “bearing his cross went forth” (John 19:17).
The son asks where the offering is, and the father answers with the gospel a full two millennia early: “My son, God will provide himself a lamb” (Genesis 22:8) — the sentence John the Baptist completes: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).
The substitute dies with his head caught in thorns — “a ram caught in a thicket by his horns” (Genesis 22:13).
And Abraham names the place with a promise in the future tense: “In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen” (Genesis 22:14).

Hebrews then hands down the verdict on what kind of event this was:

Accounting that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead; from whence also he received him in a figure.

“In a figure” — the Greek is en parabolē: in a parable.
Scripture itself declares the event a lived parable of death and resurrection — a father receiving his only son back from the dead — staged on the very mountain where it would be fulfilled, two thousand years in advance.
That is a similitude: not a story about the truth, but the truth rehearsed.

Or take Joseph, and count the frames as they go by.
Betrayed by his brothers; stripped of his garment; sold for pieces of silver; condemned between two prisoners, of whom one was lifted up to the king’s presence and the other hanged (Genesis 40:13, 19-22 — as two would hang beside another condemned man, Luke 23:39-43); raised out of the pit to the throne; made the savior of the nations with bread; unrecognized by his own brothers.
And then the line Stephen preached to the Sanhedrin: “at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren” (Acts 7:13).
At the second coming, his brothers knew him.
Stephen told that story to the very council that had condemned his Lord, and they heard what he was saying — it is the sermon that got him killed.

Or take Rahab, whose story the generation after the apostles still read this way.
A woman in a city devoted to destruction asks the spies for a sign — “give me a true token” (Joshua 2:12) — and the token is “this line of scarlet thread in the window” (Joshua 2:18).
When the city fell, every soul in the scarlet-marked house lived (Joshua 6:25): the Passover, kept this time by a gentile household — the marked house spared in the judged city.
She did not merely survive; she entered the line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5).

Clement of Rome, writing while men who knew the apostles still lived, says the spies gave her “a sign… a scarlet thread, thereby showing beforehand that through the blood of the Lord there shall be redemption unto all them that believe,” and draws the conclusion for us: “not only faith, but prophecy, is found in the woman” (1 Clement 12).
Her life was a prophecy — the verdict is Clement’s, not mine.

Now widen the lens all the way, because the master similitude is Israel herself.
Hosea wrote of the nation’s past: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt” (Hosea 11:1) — and Matthew quotes that line as prophecy, “fulfilled” when the child Jesus comes up out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15).
A sentence about the nation’s history is cited as the Son’s future: the history itself was the similitude.

The Son thus relives the nation’s story, and where Israel fell, He stands: through the water — as all Israel was “baptized… in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2, a crossing the Sea & Waters chapter will read) — then forty days fasting in the wilderness answering Israel’s forty years (Matthew 4:2), turning the tempter away each time with words drawn from the very chapters Moses wrote about those years (Deuteronomy 8:3; 6:16; 6:13).
All of Israel’s history is written this way: lived first, fulfilled after.

Treat the histories as composed.
When Scripture tells a life in unusual detail — a fare paid, a garment stripped, a third day, a thicket of thorns — the details are not color; they are lines of a similitude, and God requireth that which is past: what has been done will be done again.
Jesus, asked to prove who He was, reached for one prophet's whole life and called it the sign.
The next chapter reads it scene by scene.
